meta.section: Psychological, Social, and Biological Foundations of Behavior
meta.method: Clean-room: written in the main session from the public content-outline topic list and the cited open sources only. No MCAT question from any provider (AAMC, Khan Academy, UWorld, Kaplan, Blueprint, Jack Westin, Princeton Review) was read while writing. All studies, names and numbers are invented.

P1.title: Napping, stress and memory for word pairs
P1.text:
Sleep is thought to help stabilize newly learned information, a process called consolidation. Researchers tested whether a short afternoon nap improves retention of verbal material, and whether acute stress during the same period affects retention.

Ninety university students aged 18 to 24, all reporting 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night, took part. At 1:00 pm, each participant studied 40 pairs of unrelated nouns (for example, lantern and river) shown one pair at a time on a screen. Participants were then shown the first word of each pair and asked to type the second, and they kept studying until they could correctly produce at least 60% of the pairs.

Participants were then randomly assigned to one of three 60-minute conditions. In the nap condition, participants lay in a darkened room while electrodes recorded their brain activity (EEG), and they were allowed to sleep. In the rest condition, participants stayed awake in a lit room and watched a documentary about coastal wildlife. In the stress condition, participants stayed awake and spent part of the hour preparing and giving a short speech to two evaluators who offered no encouraging feedback, followed by mental arithmetic under time pressure. Saliva samples for cortisol were taken just before the 60-minute period and 20 minutes after it ended.

At 5:00 pm, all participants were again shown the first word of each pair and asked to type the second. Results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1

| Condition | n | Pairs recalled at 5:00 pm (mean %) | Change in salivary cortisol (nmol/L) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nap | 30 | 78 | -1.2 |
| Rest | 30 | 66 | -0.8 |
| Stress | 30 | 64 | +6.5 |

Within the nap condition, 18 participants reached slow-wave sleep according to their EEG records. These participants recalled a mean of 84% of the pairs at 5:00 pm, compared with 69% for the 12 nap participants who did not reach that stage. On their last study test at 1:00 pm, the 18 participants who later reached slow-wave sleep had produced 86% of the pairs correctly, compared with 74% for the other 12; the two subgroups did not differ in age or in usual nightly sleep. Within the stress condition, the 15 participants with the largest cortisol increases recalled a mean of 55% of the pairs at 5:00 pm, compared with 73% for the 15 with the smallest increases. The researchers concluded that slow-wave sleep strengthens newly learned associations and that acute stress after learning interferes with their retention.

P2.title: Neighborhood income, health and daily life
P2.text:
Public health researchers have long observed that health outcomes differ between neighborhoods within the same city. A research team surveyed 2,400 adults living in 40 neighborhoods of a mid-sized city to examine how neighborhood income relates to health and to features of daily life.

Neighborhoods were grouped into four quartiles by median household income, from Quartile 1 (lowest) to Quartile 4 (highest), with ten neighborhoods and about 600 respondents in each quartile. Respondents rated their own health as excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor. They also reported how many neighbors they could ask for help in an emergency, such as needing a ride to a clinic. The team used city records to measure the distance from each respondent's home to the nearest full-service grocery store. Selected results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1

| Income quartile | Rated own health fair or poor (%) | Neighbors who could be asked for help (mean) | Distance to full-service grocery store (median, km) | Respondents in a household with a car (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (lowest) | 31 | 2.1 | 3.4 | 48 |
| 2 | 24 | 2.6 | 2.2 | 71 |
| 3 | 17 | 2.9 | 1.5 | 86 |
| 4 (highest) | 11 | 2.8 | 1.1 | 93 |

Within every quartile, respondents who named three or more neighbors they could ask for help were 5 to 7 percentage points less likely to rate their health as fair or poor than respondents who named two or fewer. In Quartile 1, 38% of respondents in households without a car rated their health as fair or poor, compared with 24% of those in households with a car. In Quartile 1, 62% of respondents rented their homes, compared with 18% in Quartile 4. The team concluded that living in a low-income neighborhood harms residents' health, partly by limiting access to resources and partly by weakening the networks residents can draw on.

questions.text: Which EEG pattern would most likely have been recorded from the 18 nap participants during the stage of sleep that the researchers linked to better recall?
options: Low-amplitude, high-frequency beta waves
Sleep spindles and K-complexes as the main features
High-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves
Alpha waves of moderate frequency and amplitude
questions.solution: Slow-wave sleep is NREM stage 3, marked by high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves. Beta waves dominate alert wakefulness and alpha waves appear in relaxed wakefulness and early stage 1. Sleep spindles and K-complexes are the hallmarks of stage 2, the stage before slow-wave sleep.

questions.text: Taking each nap subgroup's score on its last study test into account, which statement best describes how the two nap subgroups changed between 1:00 pm and 5:00 pm?
options: Both subgroups lost the same number of percentage points, so slow-wave sleep added nothing beyond their head start.
The slow-wave subgroup lost fewer percentage points, but most of its 15-point lead at 5:00 pm was already there at 1:00 pm.
The slow-wave subgroup recalled more pairs at 5:00 pm than on its last study test, while the other subgroup recalled fewer.
The other subgroup lost more than 10 percentage points, while the slow-wave subgroup lost none of the pairs it had learned.
questions.solution: The slow-wave subgroup went from 86% on its last study test to 84% at 5:00 pm (down 2 points); the other subgroup went from 74% to 69% (down 5). So the slow-wave subgroup lost fewer points, but it already led by 12 points before the nap, which is most of its 15-point lead at 5:00 pm. A is wrong (2 versus 5), C is wrong (84 is below 86), and D is wrong (the losses were 5 and 2 points).

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: Which statement about the stress condition is supported by the passage?
options: Participants whose cortisol rose least recalled more pairs, on average, than participants in the rest condition.
Every participant in the stress condition recalled fewer pairs than the average participant in the rest condition.
Recall in the stress condition was more than 10 percentage points below recall in the rest condition.
Cortisol rose during the 60-minute period in all three conditions, but most in the stress condition.
questions.solution: The 15 stress participants with the smallest cortisol increases recalled 73% of the pairs, more than the rest condition's 66%. That also rules out B. The stress condition's mean (64%) is only 2 points below the rest condition's (66%), not more than 10 (C), and cortisol fell in the nap and rest conditions (D).

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: The change in cortisol in the stress condition most likely resulted from which sequence of events?
options: The hypothalamus released corticotropin-releasing hormone, the anterior pituitary released ACTH, and the adrenal cortex released cortisol.
Sympathetic nerves stimulated the adrenal medulla, which released cortisol directly into the bloodstream.
The hypothalamus released corticotropin-releasing hormone, the posterior pituitary released ACTH, and the adrenal cortex released cortisol.
The hypothalamus released ACTH, which travelled in the blood to the adrenal cortex and caused it to release cortisol.
questions.solution: Cortisol comes from the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis: corticotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus causes the anterior pituitary to release ACTH, which makes the adrenal cortex secrete cortisol. Sympathetic nerves act on the adrenal medulla, which releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, not cortisol (B). ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary, not the posterior pituitary (C) or the hypothalamus (D).

questions.text: A colleague suggests that the nap condition recalled more pairs than the rest condition only because napping participants were less stressed. Which result reported in the passage counts most against this suggestion?
options: Cortisol fell more in the rest condition than in the nap condition.
Cortisol rose in the nap condition but fell in the rest condition.
Nap participants who reached slow-wave sleep recalled 84% of the pairs.
Cortisol fell by a similar small amount in the nap and rest conditions.
questions.solution: Cortisol changed by -1.2 nmol/L in the nap condition and -0.8 in the rest condition: both small falls, so the two conditions look similarly unstressed, yet recall differed by 12 points (78% versus 66%). That counts against stress as the explanation. A would be even stronger evidence if it were true, but the passage reports the opposite (the nap condition's fall was slightly larger), and B misstates it too (cortisol fell in both). C is reported but says nothing about stress.

questions.text: Based on the passage, how did recall at 5:00 pm compare between the 15 stress participants with the smallest cortisol increases and the 12 nap participants who did not reach slow-wave sleep?
options: The nap participants recalled about 15 percentage points more.
The two groups recalled the same percentage of pairs.
The nap participants recalled about 4 percentage points more.
The stress participants recalled about 4 percentage points more.
questions.solution: The 15 stress participants with the smallest cortisol increases recalled 73% of the pairs and the 12 nap participants who did not reach slow-wave sleep recalled 69%, so the stress participants recalled about 4 points more. C reverses the groups. The 15-point gap in A is the difference between the two nap subgroups (84% versus 69%).

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: The longer distances to full-service grocery stores in lower-income neighborhoods are best described as an example of:
options: spatial inequality.
residential segregation.
relative poverty.
social reproduction.
questions.solution: Spatial inequality is the unequal distribution of resources and services across places, such as grocery stores being farther from poorer neighborhoods. Residential segregation is the separation of social groups into different neighborhoods, which may contribute to the pattern but is not the pattern itself. Relative poverty describes having much less than others in one's society, and social reproduction describes inequality being passed from one generation to the next.

provenance.kind: standard sociology term; not defined in OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e

questions.text: Which statement best describes how the mean number of neighbors respondents could ask for help changes with neighborhood income in Table 1?
options: It rises with every step up in neighborhood income, from Quartile 1 to Quartile 4.
It rises from Quartile 1 to Quartile 2 and then stays about the same.
It rises from Quartile 1 to Quartile 3 and then dips slightly in Quartile 4.
It falls from Quartile 3 to Quartile 4 by more than it rose from Quartile 2 to Quartile 3.
questions.solution: The means are 2.1, 2.6, 2.9 and 2.8: up 0.5, up 0.3, then down 0.1. A ignores the dip, B ignores the rise from Quartile 2 to Quartile 3, and in D the dip (0.1) is smaller than the rise before it (0.3).

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: Which is the strongest objection to the team's conclusion that living in a low-income neighborhood harms residents' health?
options: With only ten neighborhoods in each quartile, there are too few neighborhoods to compare income groups.
Respondents' own incomes were not measured, so the pattern could reflect poorer people rather than poorer places.
Self-rated health is subjective and may differ from an assessment made by a physician.
The findings come from a single mid-sized city and may not hold in much larger cities.
questions.solution: Neighborhoods were sorted only by median household income; respondents' own incomes were not recorded. People with low incomes tend to have worse health wherever they live, so the pattern could come from who lives in Quartile 1 neighborhoods rather than from the neighborhoods themselves (a compositional rather than a contextual effect). Ten neighborhoods and about 600 respondents per quartile is modest but workable (A). Self-rated health is a widely used measure that tracks later illness (C). D limits how far the results generalize but does not challenge the conclusion for this city.

provenance.kind: research-design reasoning on the invented study

questions.text: Which group's rate of rating health as fair or poor was closest to the overall rate in Quartile 2?
options: Quartile 1 respondents overall
Quartile 1 respondents in households without a car
Quartile 1 respondents in households with a car
Quartile 3 respondents overall
questions.solution: Quartile 2's overall rate is 24%. Quartile 1 respondents in households with a car rated their health fair or poor at 24%, the same rate. Quartile 1 overall is 31%, Quartile 1 without a car 38%, and Quartile 3 overall 17%.

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: A city council member argues that grocery chains place stores where expected sales are highest, and that this arrangement keeps the city's food supply running efficiently as a whole even if some areas are less well served. This view most closely reflects:
options: conflict theory.
symbolic interactionism.
feminist theory.
functionalism.
questions.solution: Functionalism explains a social arrangement by the part it plays in keeping the whole system working, which is the council member's argument. Conflict theory would stress that more powerful groups shape store locations to their own advantage at others' expense. Symbolic interactionism studies the meanings people create in everyday interaction, and feminist theory examines how gender shapes social arrangements.

questions.text: Based on the passage, about what percentage of all Quartile 1 respondents lived in a household without a car and rated their health as fair or poor?
options: About 12%
About 20%
About 26%
About 31%
questions.solution: 52% of Quartile 1 respondents live in a household without a car (100 - 48), and 38% of them rated their health fair or poor: 0.52 x 0.38 = 0.198, about 20% of all Quartile 1 respondents. 12% is the matching figure for respondents with a car (0.48 x 0.24), and 31% is the rate for all Quartile 1 respondents.

provenance.kind: data reading on the invented study

questions.text: A participant can just detect that a 300 g weight has become heavier when 9 g are added to it. According to Weber's law, about how much weight must be added to a 700 g weight for the same participant to just detect the change?
options: 9 g
questions.solution: Weber's law states that the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the original stimulus. Here the fraction is 9/300 = 0.03, so for 700 g the change needed is 0.03 x 700 = 21 g. 9 g wrongly treats the difference as a fixed amount; 27 g triples 9 g instead of scaling by 700/300; 63 g treats the 9 as a percentage.

questions.text: A fitness app awards a badge after an unpredictable number of logged workouts, averaging one badge for every five workouts. Compared with awarding a badge after every workout, this schedule would most likely produce:
options: a high, steady rate of logging that continues longer once badges stop.
a pause in logging after each badge, followed by a burst of activity.
logging that speeds up as the expected time of the next badge approaches.
logging that stops more quickly once badges are no longer given.
questions.solution: A badge after an unpredictable number of responses is a variable-ratio schedule, which produces a high, steady response rate with little pause and the greatest resistance to extinction. A pause after each reward is typical of fixed-ratio schedules, and speeding up as a reward time approaches is the fixed-interval pattern. Behavior reinforced every time (continuous reinforcement) extinguishes faster, not slower.

questions.text: A clinic nurse decides that a patient who has arrived late for a third appointment does not care about his health, without considering that he depends on an unreliable bus route. The next week, when the nurse arrives late for her own shift, she blames heavy traffic. The contrast between her two explanations best illustrates:
options: the fundamental attribution error.
the self-serving bias.
the actor-observer bias.
the just-world hypothesis.
questions.solution: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to explain other people's behavior by their dispositions while explaining one's own behavior by the situation, which is exactly the contrast here. The fundamental attribution error covers only the first half (judging the patient). The self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own successes and failures and says nothing about judging others. The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve.

questions.text: According to one version of the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia, excess dopamine activity in limbic regions of the brain is most closely associated with which symptoms?
options: Delusions and reduced speech
Flat affect and social withdrawal
Disorganized speech and lack of motivation
Hallucinations and delusions
questions.solution: In this version of the hypothesis, too much dopamine activity in the limbic system is linked to positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, while too little dopamine in the prefrontal cortex is linked to negative symptoms such as reduced speech, flat affect, withdrawal and low motivation. A and C each pair a positive symptom with a negative one, and B lists only negative symptoms.

questions.text: A 14-year-old notices that her teachers seem surprised whenever she answers a science question correctly. Over the school year she comes to see herself as 'not a science person.' This change in her self-concept best illustrates:
options: the looking-glass self.
the Pygmalion effect.
identity foreclosure.
social facilitation.
questions.solution: Cooley's looking-glass self holds that people build their self-concept partly from how they believe others see them, which is what happens here. The Pygmalion effect is about others' expectations changing a person's performance, not self-concept. Identity foreclosure is committing to an identity without exploring alternatives, and social facilitation is performing simple tasks better in the presence of others.

questions.text: Before a meeting, most members of a hospital committee slightly favor delaying a new procedure until more data are available. After discussing it together, the committee votes to postpone the procedure indefinitely, a more cautious position than the members held on average beforehand. This shift best illustrates:
options: groupthink.
group polarization.
social loafing.
deindividuation.
questions.solution: Group polarization is the strengthening of a group's initial leaning after discussion: a mild preference for caution became a stronger one. Groupthink is members setting aside their own views to fit what they believe the group consensus is, which the scenario does not describe. Social loafing is reduced effort on pooled tasks, and deindividuation is a loss of self-awareness in groups.

questions.text: A country's crude death rate fell from 30 to 12 per 1,000 people over three decades as sanitation and vaccination improved, while its crude birth rate stayed near 38 per 1,000. If the country follows the path described by demographic transition theory, what is most likely to happen next?
options: The death rate will rise again until it matches the birth rate.
The birth rate will rise further as more children survive.
The birth rate will begin to fall, slowing population growth.
The population will stop growing within a few years.
questions.solution: A falling death rate with a still-high birth rate is the second stage of the demographic transition, a period of rapid growth. The theory's next stage is a falling birth rate, which slows growth. Death rates do not climb back (A), birth rates fall rather than rise (B), and population stability comes only in the final stage, after birth rates have fallen a long way (D).

questions.text: A first-year resident physician who is also the parent of a newborn finds that the hospital's overnight shifts and her child's needs make demands she cannot meet at the same time. This situation is best described as:
options: role strain.
role exit.
status inconsistency.
role conflict.
questions.solution: Role conflict arises when the demands of two or more roles are incompatible, here physician and parent. Role strain is too much demand within a single role, role exit is leaving a role, and status inconsistency is holding statuses ranked differently (for example, high education with low income).
